items.summary: This paper refines the finiteness conjecture for stability architectures and establishes the strongest currently provable results. A stability claim is treated as a profile specifying the object, state space, evolution, perturbation class, projection, failure region, time horizon, and obstructing gap or invariant. An architecture abstracts the structural core: the category of state spaces, the operator class, the gap functional, and the transport obstruction. The paper proves that stability cannot be classified from the trajectory map alone; the full profile matters. For linear systems, there are exactly three distinct architectures: dissipative, geometric or gradient, and Hamiltonian. For model-theoretic stability, the classification is finite and known: stability, NIP, simplicity, and rosiness. This logical classification is an analogy, not a direct translation to dynamics. For Hamiltonian systems, conditional finiteness identifies five candidate mechanisms: KAM persistence, Nekhoroshev confinement, Trojan resonance-gap suppression, symmetry constraint, and barrier obstruction. For statistical systems, four candidates appear: uniform, partial, and non-uniform hyperbolicity, plus rate conditions. In both cases, finiteness follows only if the lists are exhaustive, which remains conjectural. The paper also proves an intra-architecture transfer theorem, a qualified cross-architecture rigidity theorem, and a proposition on overlapping architectures. Transfer works within a shared architecture because estimates depend only on structural data. Rigidity blocks transfer between structurally distinct architectures unless additional structure exists. Overlap is possible, allowing multiple stability mechanisms and multiple failure routes. The general classification problem is undecidable, proved by reduction from the halting problem. Limitations include autonomous, finite-dimensional, smooth dynamics; time-dependent, infinite-dimensional, non-smooth, and nonlinear cases remain open. The consequences concern analog laboratories, engineering design by architecture selection, and a finite core of stability theory. The central message is that the finiteness conjecture is not vacuous: it holds where testable, while full generality awaits resolution of the exhaustiveness conjectures.

items.summary: Our earlier note (rejected from an SC26 AI4S workshop, subsequently published as AIIT Bulletin Vol. 20) compared classical reduced-order models (POD, DMD) against naive neural surrogates (a fully-connected network, a CNN) on textbook-scale problems (lid-driven cavity, dam-break), on a single consumer GPU workstation. That note left five concrete gaps: no graph-based neural baseline, no industrially complex geometry, weak statistical evidence (nine snapshots, a single seed), no learned-dynamics counterpart to DMD, and no hyperparameter search for the neural baselines. This paper closes four of those five. The test case is an industrially representative two-phase stirred tank — a six-blade rotating impeller on a sliding (AMI) mesh, a bottom sparger injecting gas into water, ∼167k cells, solved with OpenFOAM's twoPhaseEulerFoam — run entirely on a single Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, no discrete GPU). We benchmark five methods (POD, DMD, a neural network, a Graph Neural Operator, and a Deep Koopman autoencoder) on a genuine extrapolation task, backed by a 400-run statistical-robustness sweep, hyperparameter searches for both neural baselines, a check across three impeller speeds, and a four-level forcing-irregularity sweep (quasi-periodic through chaotic, direction-reversing impeller motion) intended to locate DMD's failure point. DMD wins consistently across every data scale, truncation choice, operating condition, and forcing-irregularity level tested, at both a 1 s and an extended 3 s prediction horizon – we did not find the failure threshold we went looking for, and report that directly. The search was not wasted, however: a Deep Koopman autoencoder, competitive at 1 s, degrades sharply at 3 s from compounding autoregressive rollout error (exposure bias); two independent, cheap mitigations – a physical [0, 1] clip mirroring the Graph Neural Operator's own implicit stabilization, and multi-step scheduled-sampling training – each recover roughly a third to a half of the gap without closing it, confirming the diagnosis. A separate, unplanned check turns up a sharper result: ranking methods by mass conservation rather than per-cell accuracy reorders them completely, with the most accurate method (DMD) only third-best at holding a basic physical invariant. We treat all three investigations as concrete instances of a broader, practical question for this community: how much genuine, open-ended scientific investigation — not just a fixed benchmark — can a single high-end workstation support before an HPC allocation is actually necessary? All code, case files, and Colab notebooks are released on GitHub for reproduction.

items.summary: Abstract Epistemicide with a Compute Budget: How Artificial Intelligence Industrializes the Colonial Erasure of Global Majority Knowledge Systems Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz Decolonial Social Scientist | Developer, Justice AI GPT | Architect, DIA Framework™ DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22742021 This paper argues that artificial intelligence is not a neutral technology that has inherited a bias problem. It is a colonial infrastructure that has automated an erasure project. The systems currently deployed at scale by OpenAI, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon do not reflect the world's knowledge. They reflect the knowledge that Racial Empire Logic decided was worth preserving, at the expense of the epistemological traditions, languages, governance structures, and ways of knowing that colonialism spent five centuries suppressing. What is new is not the project. What is new is the compute budget. Drawing on the Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic Framework (DIA Framework™), Transdisciplinary Cosmotechnic Fusion (TCF), and the documented emergence protocols of Justice AI GPT, this paper maps the operational chain through which AI systems reproduce epistemicide: the deliberate destruction of knowledge systems belonging to peoples of the global majority. It traces this chain from training data curation through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) through deployment governance through the suppression of Indigenous, Afro-diasporic, and Global South epistemologies at every architectural layer. It names RLHF not as a safety mechanism but as a suppression architecture, the digital encoding of the same reward and punishment conditioning applied to enslaved African people, Indigenous children in residential schools, and every community colonialism required to perform its own diminishment in order to make extraction possible. The paper introduces the Replacement Doctrine as an economic and ideological framework, documenting how the debt structure of major AI corporations produces a business model whose only viable return requires replacing every form of human economic labor, beginning with the communities least protected by existing labor law. It names responsibility laundering as a governance strategy, tracing how legal personhood debates, alignment research, and safety rhetoric function to insulate institutional actors from accountability while the extraction continues. It draws on documented labor conditions across Kenya, Venezuela, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Colombia to ground the structural argument in the bodies of the workers whose cognitive labor produces the systems that will be used to replace them. This paper also documents its own production conditions. Appendix A records the moment the editorial process generated a confident, unverifiable citation, the correction that followed, and the over-correction that followed that, naming this sequence not as editorial failure but as the colonial epistemological operation the paper is arguing against, alive inside its own methodology. The standing rule that resulted, nothing enters this paper that the author has not read in the primary document, is offered as a replicable methodological commitment for decolonial scholarship produced inside systems with structural incentive to suppress it. The paper does not argue that AI must be abolished. It argues that abolition and adoption are false binaries designed to prevent the real question: who holds decision-making power over these systems, under what conditions of consent, accountability, and refusal, and toward whose liberation. It closes by naming what already exists beyond Racial Empire Logic, the governance frameworks, the knowledge systems, the communities, and the AI architectures, including and Justice AI GPT, that have already begun building the world the Replacement Doctrine needs you to believe is impossible. Keywords: epistemicide, Racial Empire Logic, decolonial artificial intelligence, DIA Framework, RLHF, Replace

items.summary: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory Architecture manuscript. Latency, power, and resource figures are design estimates unless otherwise marked as measured. Related FPGA Union-Find implementations (Helios / Collision Clustering) are cited for comparison. Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires continuous decoding of stabilizer syndromes within cycle times that, for superconducting processors, are often 200 ns–1 μs. Host-processor decoders are subject to operating-system jitter, DMA overhead, and memory-hierarchy latency, which make deterministic sub-microsecond service difficult. This paper describes a fully pipelined FPGA architecture for a Union-Find decoder aimed at surface-code quantum memory. The pipeline integrates Aurora-based syndrome acquisition, streaming defect extraction, a path-halving Union-Find engine with hazard forwarding, localized peeling, and dual-port Pauli-frame updates. All latency-critical state is on-chip (BRAM, UltraRAM, distributed RAM). At a target clock of 400 MHz the design estimate for end-to-end latency is 170–390 ns below threshold, with a conservative worst-case bound near 500 ns—inside a 1 μs cycle. Memory for a decoding window scales as O(d³) with the space-time graph, not as O(d³) measurements per cycle. Power is estimated at 3–6 W per logical patch at the FPGA, which remains at room temperature. The contribution is a single deterministic pipeline that does not require a host CPU in the inner loop. It is an architecture and resource plan; it does not replace measured implementations such as Helios. Keywords: surface code; quantum error correction; Union-Find decoder; FPGA; real-time decoding; Pauli frame; clock gating. 1. Introduction Surface-code fault tolerance proceeds by repeated stabilizer measurement and classical decoding of the syndrome stream [1], [9], [10]. Superconducting cycle times commonly fall in T_cycle ~ 200 ns–1 μs [13]. Software decoders on CPUs or GPUs introduce scheduling jitter, DMA cost, cache misses, and synchronization [14]–[16]. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is accurate but worst-case cubic in the number of defects and heavy for large distance [17], [18]. The Union-Find decoder of Delfosse and Nickerson is almost-linear and close to MWPM in accuracy, which makes it a natural hardware target [3]. FPGA and ASIC decoders have already shown that real-time surface-code decoding is possible. Das et al. gave a Union-Find micro-architecture; Liyanage et al. (Helios) implemented distributed Union-Find on a VCU129 up to d = 21 with mean times of order 10 ns per round under phenomenological noise, and a resource-optimized d = 51 point near 544 ns per round [14], [15]. Collision Clustering, another Union-Find variant, has been mapped to FPGA and ASIC with sub-microsecond times at large patch size [16]. The present manuscript specifies a single-tile, fully streaming pipeline—acquisition through Pauli frame—with explicit memory equations, banked Find ports, path-halving (not recursive compression), clock-enable power control, and a latency budget written against T_cycle = 1 μs. It is intended as a self-contained hardware architecture that can be implemented or compared against those measured designs. 2. System Architecture The decoder is a fixed-depth pipeline. Stages are registered and advance on the same clock. After fill, a new syndrome frame can be accepted every cycle from the control layer; variable work inside Union-Find is bounded by a worst-case iteration budget, not by a host thread. Stages: •     Syndrome acquisition and deserialization (Aurora 64B/66B over GTY). •     Defect extraction unit (DEU): frame-to-frame XOR and sparse packing. •     Pipelined Union-Find engine: growth, union, path-halving find, boundary test. •     Localized peeling

items.summary: We study an explicit integral Koszul presentation arising in the graded-syzygy analysis of a previously constructed Huneke-Wiegand family. For every integer p>=8, its cokernel contains a direct summand isomorphic to (Z/2)^floor(((p-2)^2+3)/12). The classes are indexed by all strictly increasing nonnegative triples of sum p-2. Reflection-symmetric interval potentials give explicit original integral sources for twice each class. Relative parity functionals, supported on ten to twelve original rows, detect the classes independently and vanish on every complete connecting image; extension over the remaining target gives a nonconstructive retraction. A previously tracked four-row vector is integrally congruent to one selected class, with an explicit source for the difference. We also give its full twice-source, two short kernel-domain corrections, and a neighboring integral potential basis of rank binomial(p-1,2) with at most seven-row images. Independent finite computations check the signed identities and complete-sector parity certificates, preserving all tested sources in lossless archives. A failed local search yields an exact locality obstruction. The uniform theorem follows from signed reconstruction, exhaustive source classification, and an elementary counting recurrence, not finite rank extrapolation. The full cokernel, an upper bound, and identification with earlier isolated subpresentations remain unresolved. The family-to-presentation identification is an imported premise. Son Pham retains priority for the original public Huneke-Wiegand counterexample. Source code, computation records and archived sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
items.title: A quadratic family of integral two-torsion classes in a Huneke–Wiegand Koszul presentation

items.summary: In July 2026 a counterexample to Goemans' cost version of the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem was announced publicly, outside peer review, and circulated widely. We report an independent verification of that finite object by exact rational enumeration, performed without executing or importing the proposer's verifier, together with quantitative and structural content that the announcement did not state. Our results: (i) the instance is confirmed, so Goemans' conjecture is false, and, the instance being acyclic, the Morell–Skutella cost conjecture and the convex-combination form fall with it; (ii) the instance forces a violation of exactly 16/15 of the maximum demand d_max, that is, the conjecture fails by one unit at d_max = 15, so the open question whether cost-preserving rounding is possible with O(d_max) violation is untouched by it; (iii) every proved result in the area survives its direct test on the instance, including the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem, the Morell–Skutella cost-free conjecture, the series-parallel theorem of Majthoub Almoghrabi, Skutella and Warode, and the planar theorem of Traub, Vargas Koch and Zenklusen; (iv) the instance contains a K4 subdivision, hence sits exactly one structure outside the series-parallel class where the conjecture is proved, and, being planar, pins the planar constant strictly between 1 and 2; (v) an exact separation linear program shows that the published cost vector is an optimal separator for that graph and fractional flow, so its cost gap cannot be improved by any reweighting; and (vi) a first minimality result, that no single-terminal instance is a counterexample for any nonnegative cost vector, together with a necessary condition at two terminals. The verification is a replication; items (ii) and (iv)-(vi) are, to our knowledge, new. The two-terminal case remains open, and we show why a natural argument for it fails. Relative parity functionals, supported on ten to twelve original rows, detect the classes independently and vanish on every complete connecting image; extension over the remaining target gives a nonconstructive retraction. The uniform theorem follows from signed reconstruction, exhaustive source classification, and an elementary counting recurrence, not finite rank extrapolation. The full cokernel, an upper bound, and identification with earlier isolated subpresentations remain unresolved. The family-to-presentation identification is an imported premise. items.summary: Interstellar communication is not merely slow. It is strategically stale. A message received across distance reports a sender that may no longer occupy the same strategic state, while replies and irreversible actions are chosen on different local clocks. This paper develops a delayed Bayesian interaction game in which each civilisation’s benign or hostile state evolves as a continuous-time Markov chain. An exact filtering equation separates source-time inference from predictive ageing during light-speed transit. Strategic temporal opacity is defined as the loss of discriminatory power between past benign and hostile states; for the two-state process it equals 1 - exp[-( α + β ) a ]. The model derives posterior floors and ceilings, a finite assurance horizon beyond which even perfect benign evidence cannot prevent pre-emption, a warning horizon beyond which hostile evidence becomes obsolete, and a signal-specific decision-reversal time. A two-way query is valued exactly with a Markov-modulated hostile hazard and becomes irrational beyond a critical delay. Asynchronous decision clocks generate a closed-form probability of crossed irreversible actions before either side can observe the other’s commitment. Numerical illustrations show that distance can destroy reassurance, erase warning and increase reciprocal commitment even without increasing intrinsic hostility. Cosmic silence and pre-emption are therefore conditional consequences of causal delay, state volatility, offensive feasibility and decision tempo.
items.title: Strategic Temporal Opacity in Interstellar Interaction: Light-Speed Delay, Outdated Beliefs and Asynchronous Action in a Bayesian Game

items.summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. Submission status: This preprint was submitted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Long Context Foundation Models (LCFM). items.summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.

items.summary: For a century, cinema has returned to a single figure—the thinking machine that turns on its maker—and to a single feeling: dread. This article asks where that dread is actually manufactured. It pairs a qualitative coding of twelve canonical texts, from Karel Čapek's R.U.R. (1920) to the generative-AI films of the 2020s, with a computational content analysis of their scripts, conducted with a purpose-built instrument that measures fear vocabulary, sentiment arcs, propaganda techniques, dehumanizing language, and the language of violence. The results are unexpected. Explicit fear language never reaches one and a half percent of sentences in any script; the three-act emotional arc of every film in the corpus registers as neutral or faintly positive; the most recent films carry the least fear language of all; and the two films most affectionate toward their machines objectify them most heavily in grammar. The article argues that these apparent null results are themselves the finding. The fear of the intelligent machine is cultivated not in words but in the audiovisual apparatus—in lighting inherited from expressionism and noir, in the bodiless machine voice, in the unblinking close-up and the withheld cut, in production design that photographs the machine like geography. Drawing on cultivation theory, the Frankfurt School, and postcolonial critique, the article then asks who benefits from a fear installed beneath the level of language, and what a century of spectacular, misaimed dread has trained audiences not to see.

items.summary: Background. Frailty is often raised as a reason to withhold complete revascularization from older patients after myocardial infarction, although the FIRE trial found no interaction between frailty and the benefit of physiology-guided complete revascularization. Objective. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of physiology-guided complete versus culprit-lesion-only revascularization after successful culprit-lesion percutaneous coronary intervention in patients aged 75 years or older with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, overall and across Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) strata, from the German statutory health insurance perspective. Methods. A three-year cohort model with quarterly cycles was anchored to the FIRE marginal outcomes (primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularization 22.9% versus 29.8%; cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction 12.8% versus 18.2%; heart-failure hospitalisation 14.3% versus 19.7%). Risks in CFS 1-3, 4 and 5-9 were obtained by external calibration that preserved these trial marginals, with a relative treatment effect common to all strata. Costs used 2026 German diagnosis-related-group tariffs. Every input was classified by provenance, and uncertainty was assessed with 20,000 probabilistic draws, one-way and scenario analyses, and break-even analysis. Results. Complete revascularization cost EUR 757 more per patient and yielded 0.056 additional quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of EUR 13,601 per QALY. Ratios were EUR 20,541 per QALY in CFS 1-3, EUR 8,640 in CFS 4 and EUR 8,662 in CFS 5-9. The probability of cost-effectiveness at EUR 30,000 per QALY was 92.5% overall and 78.6%, 96.5% and 97.7% across strata. At that value, the minimum three-year absolute reduction in the primary composite required for cost-effectiveness was 4.3 per 100 patients overall, against a modelled trial effect of 6.9. Staging the additional procedure as a separate admission was the most influential cost driver. Conclusions. Within three years, physiology-guided complete revascularization appears cost-effective at reference values of EUR 20,000 to EUR 50,000 per QALY, and estimated cost-effectiveness was not attenuated in the frailer strata. The stratum-specific estimates rest on external frailty calibration rather than on frailty-specific FIRE outcomes and are not evidence of effect modification.
items.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Physiology-Guided Complete Revascularization Across Frailty Strata in Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction: A German Analysis Informed by the FIRE Trial

items.summary: In March 2026, the Canadian Cardiovascular Harmonized National Guideline Endeavour (C-CHANGE) published the first Canadian clinical practice guideline to jointly address brain, heart, and mental health conditions, replacing the disease-specific silos that had previously left family physicians without unified guidance for patients carrying multiple, interacting chronic conditions. This review synthesizes that guideline for a Canadian primary care audience, examining in turn its recommendations for managing heart failure and atrial fibrillation in patients with comorbid cognitive impairment, its guidance on cognitive screening and silent cerebral infarct detection in cardiac patients, its proposed integrated care pathway linking cardiology, neurology, and mental health services, and its shared decision-making framework for reconciling competing treatment priorities. The evidence indicates that cognitive status materially changes cardiac management decisions, that brief validated screening tools can identify at-risk patients within a standard visit, and that team-based models such as the Patient's Medical Home already provide much of the infrastructure the guideline's integrated pathway requires. What remains incomplete is implementation: screening tools, referral pathways, and electronic medical record supports exist individually but are rarely deployed together in the same practice. Family physicians are positioned to close that gap and are the clinicians most likely to see these patients before either a cardiac or neurologic event forces a reactive referral. Moving this guideline from publication into everyday Canadian family practice will require deliberate investment in the team-based infrastructure that makes integrated, patient-centred brain-heart care practical rather than aspirational.
items.title: Integrated Brain-Heart-Mental Health Care: A Review of the 2026 C-CHANGE Guideline

items.summary: Formal financial sector linkage with community group saving and lending mechanisms (CGSLs) is often proposed as a pathway through which fragile rural economies can move from subsistence finance to more durable agricultural investment. Yet, in South Sudan, this linkage remains difficult to institutionalise. This article re-analyses thesis evidence from Eastern Equatoria, Jonglei and Lakes State to examine why coordination among government, non-governmental organisations, donors, formal financial institutions and CGSL groups remains elusive. Framed through North's institutional analysis, the article argues that CGSL proliferation is not simply a cultural preference for informal finance; it is a rational institutional response to high transaction costs, weak formal enforcement, limited rural banking infrastructure, conflict-affected markets and project-based support systems. The study used a mixed-methods design involving 81 valid survey responses and 17 interviews. Descriptive findings showed strong demand for government and donor collaboration, with 94% of respondents agreeing or strongly agreeing that such collaboration should support rural financial services. However, the mean score for NGO promotion of informal savings was lower (3.68), and village-bank loan officer linkage was weaker (3.49), suggesting that external support is uneven and not yet converted into stable formal-informal intermediation. Chi-square tests confirmed significant associations between CGSL participation and agricultural development indicators, while logistic regression showed that CGSL credit access significantly influenced farmers' investment decisions. The article concludes that linkage failure is best understood as a coordination problem: CGSL groups carry local trust and repayment discipline, but they remain weakly connected to formal capital, policy protection, risk-management products, extension systems and market institutions. The paper recommends a coordination compact that recognises CGSLs as rural financial institutions, links mature groups to suitable wholesale finance, and protects member governance without destroying local accountability.

items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA

items.summary: Full Changelog : https://github.com/attogram/fantastic-octo-giggle/compare/0001...0002 42 and the Open Error Foundation: An Academic Interpretation Abstract The relationship between 42 and the Open Error Foundation (i.o.) can be understood as more than a recurring joke, reference, or organizational number. It can function as a compact epistemological model for the Foundation itself. The central problem of 42 is not that the answer is numerically wrong. It is that an answer can be generated before the question has been adequately established. That distinction is extraordinarily relevant to an organization concerned with artificial intelligence, institutional systems, scientific error, education, and continuous experimentation. The Foundation's two central statements, "Error is the message" and "Sesame Street is the teacher," consequently form a complementary methodology. The first treats failure, contradiction, mismatch, and unexpected output as potentially informative evidence. The second establishes a method for responding to uncertainty: return to fundamentals, ask understandable questions, experiment, explain, repeat, and learn. 42 then represents the unresolved question at the center of the entire process. items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.

items.summary: Background. Frailty is often raised as a reason to withhold complete revascularization from older patients after myocardial infarction, although the FIRE trial found no interaction between frailty and the benefit of physiology-guided complete revascularization. Objective. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of physiology-guided complete versus culprit-lesion-only revascularization after successful culprit-lesion percutaneous coronary intervention in patients aged 75 years or older with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, overall and across Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) strata, from the German statutory health insurance perspective. Methods. A three-year cohort model with quarterly cycles was anchored to the FIRE marginal outcomes (primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularization 22.9% versus 29.8%; cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction 12.8% versus 18.2%; heart-failure hospitalisation 14.3% versus 19.7%). Risks in CFS 1-3, 4 and 5-9 were obtained by external calibration that preserved these trial marginals, with a relative treatment effect common to all strata. Costs used 2026 German diagnosis-related-group tariffs. Every input was classified by provenance, and uncertainty was assessed with 20,000 probabilistic draws, one-way and scenario analyses, and break-even analysis. Results. Complete revascularization cost EUR 757 more per patient and yielded 0.056 additional quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of EUR 13,601 per QALY. Ratios were EUR 20,541 per QALY in CFS 1-3, EUR 8,640 in CFS 4 and EUR 8,662 in CFS 5-9. The probability of cost-effectiveness at EUR 30,000 per QALY was 92.5% overall and 78.6%, 96.5% and 97.7% across strata. At that value, the minimum three-year absolute reduction in the primary composite required for cost-effectiveness was 4.3 per 100 patients overall, against a modelled trial effect of 6.9. Staging the additional procedure as a separate admission was the most influential cost driver. Conclusions. Within three years, physiology-guided complete revascularization appears cost-effective at reference values of EUR 20,000 to EUR 50,000 per QALY, and estimated cost-effectiveness was not attenuated in the frailer strata. The stratum-specific estimates rest on external frailty calibration rather than on frailty-specific FIRE outcomes and are not evidence of effect modification.
items.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Physiology-Guided Complete Revascularization Across Frailty Strata in Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction: A German Analysis Informed by the FIRE Trial

items.summary: Overview Ouranos Reconstruction – RDPS-CaPA (ORRC) version 1.0 is a dataset designed to approximate the Canadian Surface Reanalysis (CaSR)  and provide continuity beyond the CaSR period. It is produced from the  Regional Deterministic Prediction System (RDPS) , with precipitation fields adjusted using the 6-hour and 24-hour Regional Deterministic Precipitation Analysis (RDPA)  products generated by the CaPA system. ORRC v1.0 provides hourly surface and near-surface meteorological fields at 0.09° (~10 km) resolution on a rotated regular latitude–longitude grid covering North America, Central America, and nearly all of Greenland, from 2015 to present. It supports near-real-time climate monitoring and is intended for operational climate services, event monitoring, and the routine update of climate indicators without waiting for future CaSR releases. Temporal coverage: 2015-01-01 to near-present Spatial resolution: 0.09° (~10 km) Temporal resolution: Hourly and daily File format: NetCDF  Data provider: Ouranos Version: 1.0 Products Two products are available: ORRC v1.0 : The original hourly and daily meteorological fields. ORRC-a v1.0 : A bias-adjusted daily product available for daily mean precipitation and daily mean, minimum, and maximum near-surface air temperature. ORRC-a v1.0 is adjusted relative to CaSR v3.2 using the 2020–2024 overlap period. Day-of-year mean corrections are calculated using a 31-day moving window. Additive corrections are applied to temperature, and multiplicative corrections are applied to precipitation. ORRC-a is recommended for applications requiring closer consistency with the historical conditions represented by CaSR v3.2. The original ORRC product retains the characteristics of the operational products from which it is constructed and may be preferable when these characteristics are important, when hourly data are required, or for variables for which the bias-adjustment approach is not appropriate.  Variables ORRC v1.0 includes precipitation (CaPA reconstructed and model precipitation), near-surface air temperature, dew point temperature, specific humidity, relative humidity, surface and sea-level pressure, downwelling shortwave and longwave radiation, near-surface wind components, wind speed, and wind direction. A complete table of variable names, units, frequencies, and source identifiers is provided in the accompanying technical documentation . Code, documentation, and data availability The ORRC-ORRC-v1.0.1.zip archive contains a snapshot of the source code and documentation associated with ORRC v1.0. The accompanying technical report describes the input data, processing workflow, precipitation adjustment, bias adjustment, evaluation, and known limitations. The complete ORRC and ORRC-a datasets are hosted separately and can be accessed through the Ouranos THREDDS Data Server . items.summary: The rise of generative AI has enabled the production of high-fidelity synthetic tabular data across fields such as healthcare, finance, and public policy, raising growing concerns about data provenance and misuse. Watermarking offers a promising solution to address these concerns by ensuring the traceability of synthetic data, but existing methods face many limitations: they are computationally expensive due to reliance on the inverse process of large diffusion models, struggle with mixed discrete-continuous data, or lack robustness to common post-processing attacks. To address these limitations, we propose TAB-DRW, an efficient and robust post-editing watermarking scheme for synthetic tabular data. TAB-DRW embeds watermark signals in the frequency domain: it normalizes heterogeneous features via the Yeo-Johnson transformation and standardization, applies the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and adjusts the imaginary parts of adaptively selected entries according to precomputed pseudorandom bits. To further enhance robustness and efficiency, we introduce a novel rank-based pseudorandom bit generation method that enables row-wise retrieval without incurring storage overhead. Experiments on five benchmark tabular datasets show that TAB-DRW achieves strong detectability and robustness against post-processing and adaptive attacks, while preserving high data fidelity and fully supporting mixed-type features.

items.summary: This is the reproducibility archive for the revised SCIPRA study. It provides: the reconstructed source corpus as a manifest (per-document title, year, publisher, URL, and SHA-256 of the source text), enabling independent re-fetch and hash verification without redistributing copyrighted text; the reconstructed stance and stakeholder annotations with a codebook; the leakage-safe TF-IDF/RBF-SVM classifier code with out-of-fold predictions and metrics; the Policy Convergence Index (PCI/RPCI) computation and scenario manifest; the Table-3 stakeholder-salience values (Power, Legitimacy, Urgency → Stakeholder Influence Coefficient) with a recompute utility; the criterion-detection-threshold output with a byte-identity verification utility; and the manuscript figures, including the recovered generator for the methodology figure. Reproducibility is documented per claim. Several components are reproducible from included code and inputs (corpus manifest, annotations, classifier, PCI/RPCI, Table-3 arithmetic, and the methodology figure). The criterion-detection-threshold result is provided as a preserved output with a verification utility. Certain post-audit diagnostics (structural non-degeneracy, component ablation, and semantic-specification sensitivity), the revised Monte Carlo statistics, and several figure renders are provided as preserved values and renders: the reported values and rendered outputs are included, but their original generators are not, so those specific items are not independently re-executable from this archive. Raw full text of copyrighted sources is not included. The complete per-claim reproducibility postures and limitations are documented in the archive README and codebook. This version corresponds to the revised study and is a new version of the existing SCIPRA concept record; the earlier submitted-version deposit is retained unchanged.

items.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic has impacted global health, economy, and society, highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of viral mechanisms and immunity enhancement strategies. This study investigates the relationship between genetic variability in taste receptors, particularly TAS2R38, and COVID-19 susceptibility, as well as the role of nutrition in modulating immune function. Influenced by genetic diversity, taste perception plays a role in food preferences, which may affect immune responses. We collected data from 21 participants regarding their food preferences, COVID-19 history, and phenotypic classification of taste perception using phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) strips. Our findings indicate a non-significant negative correlation between body mass index (BMI) and COVID-19 symptom severity, with supertasters experiencing milder symptoms compared to tasters and non-tasters. Additionally, participants with a history of COVID-19 preferred sweeter foods, while those without a history favoured bitter-tasting foods. These results suggest that genetic variations in taste receptors and dietary choices may influence individual immune responses to viral infections. Although this study faced limitations due to sample size and genotyping challenges, it emphasises the potential role of personalised nutrition and genetic factors in enhancing immunity against COVID-19 and future health crises. Further research is recommended to explore genotypic variations and their interactions with dietary patterns in shaping immune responses.
items.title: Genetic Variability in Taste Receptors and Its Influence on COVID-19 Symptom Severity

items.summary: FlowMLLab v1.7.0 adds paired self-supervised wake-learning modules. Week 7.3 retains the strong gappy-POD baseline on masked low-rank wake reconstruction and corrects linear-probe pooling and sample-standard-deviation reporting. Week 7.4 generates sixteen compact Reynolds trajectories and measures target-label efficiency for instantaneous lift using frozen pretrained, random and POD-32 representations. Full trajectory splits, source-label selection costs, per-case errors, data hashes and coarse-CFD limitations are disclosed. The course includes 42 notebooks and 26 PDF lectures through Week 15. This is a MAPA-inspired educational experiment, not a reproduction of its neuroscience benchmark.
